analysis.one_liner: Bans the biggest online platforms from favoring their own products over competitors'.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House bill targeting the largest tech platforms cleared committee with 47 cosponsors but never reached the House floor before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for the largest online platforms — defined by size thresholds that capture companies with over $600 billion in sales or market value — to favor their own products over competitors', to use data generated by businesses on their platforms against those businesses, or to punish sellers who complain to law enforcement. Enforcement would fall to the FTC and Justice Department, with penalties up to 15 percent of a company's U.S. revenue, possible divestitures, and a private right of action for injured businesses. It cleared the House Judiciary Committee but the full House never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses and developers that sell through Amazon, Apple's App Store, Google, and similar platforms would gain tools to fight being buried in search results, having their data used to launch competing products, or being charged for unrelated services as a condition of access. Consumers would benefit indirectly through more choice and lower prices if platform gatekeeping were curbed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small businesses selling on big platforms

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered platforms from self-preferencing their own products in search, ranking, and placement, and from disadvantaging rival businesses on the platform.
Bars platforms from using nonpublic data generated by business users to build competing products, and requires data portability so sellers can leave with their own data.

Prevents platforms from forcing businesses to buy other platform services as a condition of access, from blocking interoperability, and from retaliating against anyone who reports potential violations to law enforcement.

Attaches real teeth: civil penalties up to the greater of 15 percent of U.S. revenue or 30 percent of the affected line of business's revenue, potential divestiture of conflicted lines of business, forfeiture of executive pay for repeat offenders, treble damages for injured businesses, and fast 120-day emergency injunctions.

analysis.who_pays: The handful of trillion-dollar platforms the size thresholds capture — most visibly Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta — would face fines measured in percentages of U.S. revenue, restrictions on using platform data, possible forced divestitures of lines of business like ad tech or device services, and personal pay forfeiture for repeat-offending executives. Consumers who value tightly integrated ecosystems (defaults, preinstalled apps, bundled features) would see some of that convenience loosened.

drawbacks.text: The bill as written covers any platform meeting the size thresholds regardless of who owns it, including foreign-owned apps like TikTok; critics in both parties argued this hands enforcement leverage to platforms controlled by foreign adversaries, and a committee amendment to address foreign ownership fell short.

The bill is built around a self-preferencing ban rather than a case-by-case showing of consumer harm, which defenders of the platforms argue could force companies to stop integrating features users like — preinstalled apps, default settings, bundled services — or expose them to litigation over routine product decisions; the bill's affirmative defenses for privacy and legal compliance acknowledge but do not eliminate this risk.

Compliance and litigation costs would be enormous and ultimately borne partly by users, either through changes to free services or through the platforms' continued spending on lobbying and legal defense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — stopping dominant platforms from using gatekeeper power against the businesses that depend on them — addresses a real, documented competitive problem, and the bill's size thresholds mean it only binds a handful of firms rather than every tech company. The main honest costs are that a blunt self-preferencing ban could entangle routine product decisions in litigation, and that the bill's failure to exclude foreign-owned platforms left a genuine national-security objection unanswered. A better-designed bill might have resolved both; instead, the objections became the stated reason for letting it die.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House Judiciary Committee twice and was placed on the House calendar in December 2022, but House leadership never scheduled a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in June 2021 by Rep. Cicilline with bipartisan co-sponsorship including Reps. Buck, Gooden, and Nadler, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee held markup sessions in June 2021 and ordered the bill reported as amended.

After sitting for 18 months, the committee formally reported the amended bill on December 21, 2022 (H. Rept. 117-655) and it was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills awaiting a floor vote.
The bill attracted 47 cosponsors, 38 Democrats and 9 Republicans, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the House ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest online platforms, which had lobbied heavily against the bill, are better off: it never received a floor vote, so self-preferencing and the other practices it banned remain lawful. Members who could tell constituents they supported the bill also kept a talking point without ever having to cast a deciding vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big platforms that kept it off the floor

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.role: Chair, House Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial and Administrative Law; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through the antitrust subcommittee to committee markup.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; as chair, presided over markup sessions and reported the amended bill out of committee in December 2022.

for.name: Rep. Ken Buck
for.role: House Judiciary Committee member, antitrust subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor and the bill's leading Republican advocate.

for.name: 47 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including House Majority Whip-elect Jeffries and members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the Freedom Caucus wing of Judiciary.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a floor vote on the bill, even after it was reported and placed on the House calendar in December 2022.

against.name: Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta
against.role: The covered platforms the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained lobbying campaign against the antitrust package, arguing it would harm privacy, security, and small businesses and would benefit foreign rivals like TikTok.

against.name: Members opposed on national-security grounds
against.role: Bipartisan House critics of the foreign-platform coverage
against.what_they_did: Pushed and opposed amendments in committee, including a failed amendment to tighten coverage of platforms owned by foreign adversaries, arguing the bill as drafted covered TikTok.

sides.party_line_note: Support split both parties — 38 Democrats and 9 Republicans cosponsored — and the opposition that mattered, House leadership's decision not to schedule a vote, also came from within the sponsoring party rather than along party lines.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta)
industries.note: The bill is aimed squarely at firms above $600 billion in market value with 50 million-plus U.S. users, exposing them to fines of up to 15 percent of U.S. revenue, possible divestiture of conflicted lines of business, and executive pay forfeiture for repeat violations. Their business model profits from being the gatekeeper between sellers and customers, so their interest in defeating the bill ran against the sellers and consumers the bill was written for.

industries.industry: Third-party sellers, app developers, and merchants on large platforms
industries.note: Millions of small and mid-sized businesses would get guaranteed non-discriminatory treatment, data portability, interoperability, and treble damages when platforms self-preference against them. These are the same interests as consumers, since lower seller costs translate into more choice and lower prices.

industries.industry: Antitrust enforcement agencies (FTC and DOJ Antitrust Division)
industries.note: The bill would hand the FTC and Justice Department new enforcement powers, a new Bureau of Digital Markets, and joint rulemaking over covered-platform designations, expanding their capacity to police platform markets.
